newsitem.title: CANADA: INSTANT VIEW - Canada CPI rises 2.2 pct on year.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Canada CPI rises 2.2 pct on year.

text.p: Following are reactions to December consumer price data released by Statistics Canada on Friday. Canada's unadjusted December consumer price index remained unchanged on the month and rose 2.2 percent on the year to 136.8, Statistics Canada said Thursday.
Economists in a Reuters survey had forecast, on average, the all-items consumer price index to rise 1.95 percent year-over-year.
Mark Mullins, chief economist, Midland Walwyn - "You are still seeing a bit of a pick-up in the year-over-year numbers.

Mullins - "We are definitely going to stay at, or slightly above, the midpoint of the Bank of Canada (inflation target) range. With these kinds of increases, as you get out to next summer and next autumn, you could potentially get up to 2.5 percent year-over-year or 2.7 (percent) year-over-year.
"Certainly with the underpinning that we are getting a bit of inflation out of the U.S., I would say the bias is up here in terms of core rates and overall CPI.
"All that is simply to say there is simply no more room for monetary easing."

Doug Porter, economist, Nesbitt Burns Inc - "I would say that the overall number was pretty much as expected. But core inflation was a little bit higher than we had anticipated and I would put this down to the fact that it appears the Christmas season was fairly strong and there was less discounting than usual in December.
"This is just another indication that the economy has turned the corner."

Andrew Spence, senior economist, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell - "Obviously a 0.2 percent increase in seasonally adjusted (on the month) was a little stronger I think than the market was looking for and the 2.2 percent year-over-year increase.
"But the core was unchanged (on the month) suggesting to me that despite acceleration in demand we have seen in the fourth quarter, it's clearly not a problem for inflation at the moment.
"However, one has to bear in mind that monetary policy is easing passively. That is, that as inflation moves up, real short-term interest rates come down.
"So real interest rates are easing as demand is picking up has to make me think the Bank of Canada is not going to be offsetting any future strength in the exchange rate.
"I think the Bank of Canada is poised to accept a trend to tightening in monetary conditions via the exchange rate."
